summary:
Yaroslavl Oblast stands under the national framework of Russia, where legal gender recognition, gender-marker changes on official documents and trans-specific healthcare have been prohibited since 2023. Same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned outright, so a transgender visitor cannot obtain or amend documents reflecting their gender in Russia and has no lawful route to gender-affirming care while in the country.

The 2013 'gay propaganda' statute is punishable by administrative fines of up to 400,000 rubles for individuals or detention of up to 15 days, with repeated offences escalating to criminal prosecution and up to four years' imprisonment. Following the November 2023 Supreme Court designation of the international LGBT+ movement as extremist, participation carries two to six years' imprisonment and organising carries six to ten years under Article 282.2 of the criminal code.

Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions as of 30 June 2025, approximately 98 administrative and three criminal, for alleged participation in the designated movement or for displaying its symbols. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges, including three publishing-house staff charged in May 2025 under Article 282.2 who each face up to 12 years' imprisonment; 81 people were found guilty across 98 administrative cases under Article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Russia (June 2025) records at least 139 people in Russia impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024, and assesses that openly LGBT+ people are likely to face discriminatory treatment that, by its nature or repetition, may amount to persecution, with the state able but not willing to provide protection.

The only regional deviation from this national position in Yaroslavl Oblast is the Sirotkin criminal case, opened by the regional investigative committee against an LGBTQA+ activist for participation in an extremist organisation. The charge rests on 14 social-media posts and videos of 'propaganda of non-traditional sexual relationships' published between December 2023 and January 2024, conduct of a scale that would otherwise be administrative but which the extremism framework converts into a criminal matter.
tangentialFactors:
The enforcement picture is one of rising volume as well as severity. The 101 extremism-related convictions and the 98 administrative cases under Article 20.3 are national totals, and the same charging architecture applies in Yaroslavl Oblast as in any other Russian region; the Sirotkin case is the local expression of a pattern documented across the country since the 2023 designation.

Two parallel tracks run against the same conduct. Displaying symbols or publishing material can be handled administratively under Article 20.3 or the propaganda provisions, producing fines and short detention, while the same material framed as participation in the designated extremist movement reaches Article 282.2 and multi-year sentences. The three publishing-house staff charged in May 2025, each facing up to 12 years, mark the upper end of that escalation.

The threshold for the criminal track is low enough to be met by ordinary online activity. In Yaroslavl Oblast the case file comprises 14 posts and videos accumulated over roughly two months, which indicates that a visitor or resident whose online history is examined should expect the same material to be read as evidence of extremist participation rather than as speech alone.
localsOnly:
Residents of Yaroslavl Oblast have no route to legal gender recognition: gender-marker changes on documents are prohibited and gender transition is banned, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively withdrawn in 2023. Same-sex marriage is likewise unavailable, so partners have no formal recognition of their relationship under national law.

The UK Home Office assesses that openly LGBT+ people in Russia are likely to face discriminatory treatment that, by its nature or repetition, may amount to persecution, and that the state is able but not willing to provide protection. That assessment sets the standard for UK asylum claims, and the Home Office recognises LGBT+ people in Russia as constituting a particular social group under the refugee convention.

At least 139 people in Russia were impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024 according to the same note, a figure that includes administrative fines, detention and criminal charges. Local residents in Yaroslavl Oblast face the same statutes and the same investigative bodies that opened the Sirotkin case.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory sources no enforcement data specific to Yaroslavl Oblast beyond the Sirotkin criminal case. Whether other extremism or propaganda proceedings have been opened in the oblast, and how many, is unresolved and not sourced here.

The outcome of the Sirotkin case is not sourced: no charging decision, trial date, conviction or sentence is recorded in the material available for this pass.

The figures of 101 extremism-related convictions and 139 people impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws are national aggregates and are not disaggregated by region, so no oblast-level rate can be stated. Local provision of support services, safe venues or hate-crime reporting mechanisms in Yaroslavl Oblast is not covered by the inventory and remains not sourced.
